units.title: Introduction to Computer Networks
topics: Seeing the ideas: networks, topologies, layers and delay

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: networks, topologies, layers and delay

summary: A network moves data between hosts using agreed protocols, addresses and media. LAN, MAN and WAN differ by span; the Internet is a network of networks.
Topology affects cost and reliability; today's LANs are physical stars built around switches.
Layering divides the work: each layer serves the one above and talks to its peer. OSI has seven layers, TCP/IP four.
Data is encapsulated on the way down and decapsulated on the way up; headers are overhead.
Latency = transmission + propagation + queuing + processing; BDP tells how much data fills the pipe.

units.title: The Physical Layer
topics: Telephone, cable and mobile data networks
Seeing the ideas: signals, media, multiplexing and switching

sections.title: Telephone, cable and mobile data networks
Seeing the ideas: signals, media, multiplexing and switching

summary: The physical layer moves raw bits as signals. Impairments are attenuation, distortion and noise.
Nyquist limits a noiseless channel by bandwidth and levels; Shannon limits a noisy one by bandwidth and SNR.
Line codes trade bandwidth against clock recovery: Manchester is self-clocking, NRZI and AMI are simpler.
Fibre outperforms copper in bandwidth, distance and noise immunity; UTP dominates the last 100 m.
Multiplexing shares a link by frequency, time or wavelength; switching shares a network by circuits or packets, and bursty data favours packets.

units.title: The Data Link Layer and LANs
topics: Services of the data link layer
Seeing the ideas: frames, checks, windows and shared media

sections.title: Services of the data link layer
Seeing the ideas: frames, checks, windows and shared media

summary: The data link layer frames the bit stream, detects (and may correct) errors, controls flow and arbitrates access to shared media.
Bit stuffing (HDLC) and byte stuffing (PPP) keep flags out of data. Parity is weak, the Internet checksum is cheap, CRC is strong against bursts.
Hamming codes place parity bits at powers of two; the syndrome points at the faulty bit.
Sliding-window protocols keep the pipe full; Go-Back-N is simple, Selective Repeat is efficient.
Random access (ALOHA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA) trades collisions for simplicity; switched Ethernet has replaced shared Ethernet, and Wi-Fi uses collision avoidance.

units.title: The Network Layer: Addressing and Routing
topics: Seeing the ideas: addresses, routes and the boxes that follow them

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: addresses, routes and the boxes that follow them

summary: IP is a best-effort, connectionless service; routers forward by longest-prefix match on the destination address and split oversize datagrams into fragments.
CIDR, subnetting, VLSM and aggregation allow addresses to be allocated and summarised flexibly; ARP, ICMP, DHCP and NAT make IPv4 usable; IPv6 restores the address space.
Link-state routing (Dijkstra) gives every router the same map; distance-vector routing (Bellman–Ford) shares tables with neighbours and risks count-to-infinity.
OSPF and RIP route inside an AS, BGP between ASes.

units.title: The Transport Layer
topics: Seeing the ideas: ports, segments, windows and congestion

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: ports, segments, windows and congestion

summary: The transport layer gives process-to-process delivery with ports. UDP is a thin, fast, unreliable service; TCP is a reliable byte stream.
TCP sets up with a three-way handshake, numbers bytes, acknowledges cumulatively, retransmits on timeout or three duplicate ACKs and tears down with FINs.
Flow control uses the receiver's window; congestion control uses cwnd with slow start, additive increase and multiplicative decrease.
Throughput is bounded by window / RTT, which is why high-speed long-delay paths need window scaling.

units.title: The Application Layer
topics: The World Wide Web and HTTP
Seeing the ideas: names, pages, mail, transfers and monitors

sections.title: The World Wide Web and HTTP
Seeing the ideas: names, pages, mail, transfers and monitors

summary: Application protocols are agreements over sockets: client–server or peer-to-peer, over TCP or UDP.
DNS maps names to addresses with a distributed hierarchy of servers, caching by TTL and typed records.
HTTP is a stateless text protocol; cookies add state, caching and persistent connections reduce load time; HTTPS adds TLS.
FTP separates control and data connections; SMTP pushes mail, POP3 and IMAP pull it; MIME carries binary content as Base64.
SNMP, MRTG, PRTG, Packet Tracer and Wireshark are the tools to monitor, simulate and analyse.

units.title: Network Security
topics: Seeing the ideas: ciphers, keys, hashes, handshakes and firewalls

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: ciphers, keys, hashes, handshakes and firewalls

summary: Security aims at confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication and non-repudiation; attacks are passive or active.
Symmetric ciphers (AES) are fast but need key distribution; public-key systems (RSA, Diffie–Hellman) solve distribution and give signatures; hashes provide integrity.
Certificates bind keys to names through CAs; TLS combines all of them to secure the web; IPsec and WPA2 do it at the IP and Wi-Fi layers.
Firewalls filter by policy, IDS/IPS detect and block attacks, and good practice (patching, least privilege, segmentation, MFA) matters more than any single device.
